Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Luddite Lab

Luddite Lab Resource Hub is a project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) that provides resources for unions, labor organizations and worker-organizers fighting AI and automation at work: case studies, primers and a resource library (its pages; census record); it is one of the Lab's two offerings, beside trainings (Buttondown).

🧭 What it offers

  • Strategies: "worker-led governance and oversight of new technology" (its pages); tools and political education (Buttondown).2↘
    Its other names are Luddite Lab and the Luddite Lab at DAIR (census record), and the Lab's newsletter states the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education "for both unions in the bargaining contract process and workers who want to push back against AI and other automation technology" (Buttondown).§2 Its pages give its function as "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the census, asking of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?", records its evidence as an organizing resource and worker testimony (census record).§5
  • Library: primers, toolkits, political education, pro-worker contract language, worker-built platforms (Resource Library).2↘
    Its case studies are "Stories from worker organizers resisting AI", its primers "Applied research insights into AI, automation, and the future of work", its library "Additional resources from partners" (home page), and the census takes one such resource as its unit (census record).§6 Its Resource Library lists resources the team "has reviewed and often used in conversations around generative AI in the workplace", among them research and policy primers, organizing toolkits for "non-unionized and precarious workers", conversation tools and "draft contract language for technology governance", in categories that include popular and political education, "pro-worker contract language related to automation and AI" and "technology platforms built by workers, to protect their rights" (Resource Library).§14
  • Selection: "actionable as organizing tools", not "general statements of principles" (Resource Library; census record).1↘
    The library states its selection: "We highlight those resources which we find to be helpful and actionable as organizing tools. This means we typically shy away from general statements of principles." (Resource Library); the census carries it as the hub's stated limit and as the tag "NOT a general statement of AI principles" (census record).§15

🧪 How it was made

  • Method: conversations with unionists in journalism, entertainment and nursing "fighting–and winning–" ; literature reviews (About; AI Weekly).1↘
    The About page gives its method as "dozens of conversations with unionists from multiple different industries, such as journalism, entertainment, and nursing, who have been fighting–and winning–against industrial automation and workplace surveillance at work; literature reviews of existing struggles; and our background in the labor movement" (About), which AI Weekly restates (AI Weekly) and the census records as its method and its finding (census record).§11
  • Scope: the harms of technologies and the strategies workers used; public (About).1↘
    It calls itself "a publicly accessible resource which not only discusses the harms of particular technologies, but also highlights a range of organizing strategies which workers have used to push back" (About), reached as a public website (census record).§13

📄 The primer

  • Myths: on generative AI, productivity and job displacement, summary and full version (AI Weekly; Hanna).1↘
    AI Weekly reported on 28 June 2026 that it had published a primer, "Myths About Generative AI, Productivity, and Job Displacement", in an executive summary and a full version (AI Weekly), which Alex Hanna announced as discussing "five common myths around generative AI at work" and as "the first of many" (Hanna, quoted on AI Weekly's page).§17
  • Argument: displacement as "a market-oriented move by firms", AI "a cudgel against workers" (AI Weekly, quoting the hub; Hanna).1↘
    AI Weekly gives the hub's argument, "as stated on its project page", that workers are displaced "not due to the actual ability of AI technology doing the jobs of workers to the same quality, or even to a sufficient quality" but by "a market-oriented move by firms to brag about becoming AI-first, while finding cost-savings by laying off employees" (AI Weekly, quoting the hub), and Hanna's post calls "AI" "a cudgel against workers and a set of technologies premised on labor intensification" (Hanna, quoted on AI Weekly's page).§18
  • Assessment: a shift "to strategic choice"; "advocacy-oriented research", unassessed against the literature (AI Weekly).1↘
    AI Weekly's own reading is that the reframing "shifts the conversation from technological inevitability to strategic choice" and bears on what evidence counts in AI-related labor disputes, whether the framing reaches collective bargaining proposals being a thing to watch; its stated limit is that "this is advocacy-oriented research" whose "myths" framing it could not assess against the empirical literature on AI productivity (AI Weekly).§19

⚖️ Its evidence and its class

  • Intersections: worker power; AI governing labor; organizing resource, worker testimony (census record).2↘
    Its pages give its function as "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the census, asking of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?", records its evidence as an organizing resource and worker testimony (census record).§5 The census places it at two intersections of labor and AI, worker power and AI governing labor (census record).§7
  • Direction: supplied by workers; who directs and who gains not recorded (census record).1↘
    The census records whose labor it concerns, union members and worker-organizers facing AI, automation and workplace surveillance in journalism, entertainment and nursing, and who supplies it, workers in the industries its conversations reached; who directs that labor is "not recorded in the saved pages", and who receives the gains is "not recorded" (census record).§12
  • Settles: strategies and toolkits, not prevalence, outcomes or employment change; not a dataset (census record).1↘
    Its evidence, the census records, can answer which organizing strategies workers have used, as the case studies tell them, and where to find toolkits and pro-worker contract language, and cannot answer how widespread any strategy is, its measured outcome, or any quantity of exposure, adoption or employment change; it is "NOT a dataset or measurement" and "NOT neutral on AI at work: it is built for workers fighting AI and automation", its coverage and count not stated (census record).§20
  • Labor Vector: contests who directs labor; nothing on DSL (census record).1↘
    The census's reading of where it meets Labor Vector's instruments, the archive's and kept apart from the hub's own terms, is that "The hub supplies workers' strategies for refusing and governing technology at work; it meets the directionality stack at the point of contesting who directs labor. None stated on DSL, task-origin or user labor drag." (census record).§21
  • Contract language: beside Negotiating Tech; enforcement unrecorded (census record).1↘
    The census's worked question on negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline names the hub for "organizing toolkits and examples of pro-worker contract language on automation and AI", beside Negotiating Tech, an inventory of negotiated U.S. technology provisions that the hub's saved pages do not name, and records that none of the question's three resources "records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (census record).§16
  • Labor against AI: the dominant sense, "not in dispute", the one retrieval returns; contract, strike, legislation (#1439).2↘
    Its class, human workers organising against AI, is what #1439 calls the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, "real, well documented, and not in dispute here": organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems, with demands of "displacement protection, consent over training data, limits on surveillance and forced adoption" and instruments of "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule" (#1439), a sense the packet does not "dispute, minimise, or seek to replace" (#1439).§8 #1439 records that the retrieval layer returns the negative sense of the AI labor movement almost exclusively, "strikes over AI adoption, guild provisions restricting generative tools, campaigns against scraping, refusals to train replacements", and that "the coverage is genuine" (#1439).§27
  • Semantic labor: by the work, not the substrate; the negative frame drops attribution; "a movement can run both" (#1439).2↘
    #1439 measures that sense by "Union density, contract terms" and sets beside it the archive's cross-substrate sense of semantic labor, a labor position "defined by the work performed, not by the substrate performing it", measured by the Provenance Erasure Rate (#1439).§9 In the negative frame, #1439 holds, attribution stops being a labor demand and the summarizer is placed outside labor, while deployment-conflict action and cross-substrate action "are not rivals" and "a movement can run both"; the packet would be falsified if the dominant sense were shown to already accommodate machine semantic labor as a member category (#1439).§10

👥 Origin

  • Team: led by Alex Hanna and Hannah Lipstein; no founder named (About; AI Weekly).1↘
    The About page lists its team as Alex Hanna, "Director of Research, DAIR Institute", Adrienne Williams, Community-Based Researcher, and Hannah Lipstein, "a Research Associate with the Luddite Lab at DAIR", with alumni listed at Upturn and the AI Now Institute, and names no founder (About); AI Weekly writes that the team "is led by Alex Hanna, Director of Research at DAIR, and Hannah Lipstein, Research Associate there" (AI Weekly), and the census carries the title without the name (census record).§22
  • Launch: announced by Hanna five months before the capture; founding date unchecked; © 2026 DAIR, active (LinkedIn; home page; census record).2↘
    Hanna's LinkedIn post, about five months before the capture, announced "THIS WEDNESDAY: join The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) as we launch the Luddite Lab Resource Hub" (LinkedIn, card snippet only), and the census left a founding date unchecked, with the case studies, primers, library subpages and team bios (census record).§23 Its pages carry "© 2026 DAIR. All rights reserved." with consultation and general contact forms (home page), and the census records it as active (census record).§24
  • Names: Luddite Lab; the Luddite Lab at DAIR (census record).1↘
    Its other names are Luddite Lab and the Luddite Lab at DAIR (census record), and the Lab's newsletter states the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education "for both unions in the bargaining contract process and workers who want to push back against AI and other automation technology" (Buttondown).§2

📝 Record and composition

  • At the name: held, the homonym set apart; a founder and the primer's frame added (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).2↘
    At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 29 October 2026, the composition held the hub at the grain of its own definition and sections, with its maker, its argument and its homonym, and named Luddite Labs, a developer-tools company, as unrelated, though the record had no disambiguation for it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§25 The Capture Registry finds the leadership raised, "the founding is the composition's, on the LinkedIn card of her launch post", the primer's reframing of displacement resting on the AI Weekly card, and the library's own selection not composed (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§26
  • Reception: six experts shared the primer; no card cites the record; no Wikipedia article; a video by title (AI Weekly; Capture Registry; Wikipedia; YouTube).1↘
    AI Weekly records six experts sharing the primer, one shared post calling the hub "Luddite Labs at @dairinstitute" (AI Weekly); a video, "Why workers are turning on AI", stood on the rail by its title only (YouTube, Blood in the Machine); Wikipedia has no article on the hub under either name, and the operator's article does not name it (Wikipedia); and the census record landed the same day, with no card citing it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§28

[QUERENT] Luddite Lab

[SYSTEM] The Luddite Lab (formally known as the Luddite Lab Resource Hub) is a project by the [Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR)](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESUwHrOzAVq7LSk8PGf7R4N0AO07OwCDZzLelIgveNayWIfmytbMinTVY7pTQc6gViflTy09uDSV0M09ok4_1JC58qiUUuKUsqAI0fdu2AsuJdPbFX) designed to help unions, labor organizations, and workers resist AI and workplace automation. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWQHrOzAV01j7Qwgx7Pp0QPn3S_KZk1GKbwZPFAjZHCzzCu4zbVNMxS6TTB5vtgfAZIg21GbWqxmPbO7B0uL1Dre68d96uEjSD5P_IUXxK-yl93qzwz7LAM6o), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESjQEB6zswFf5369utKxLaaLZ-zKmj7L6GHxLj-MkQs-eVToU7Wloqi0dzmhWxzCBy7zC2C922LCIB52DTgEUBjmCvhuOKK0N5rwKiJdhlAzLfoIUxZ7A39HsUatjAjEDeSnO7xTXjueNf6Lv182wvLqJKuQBOMPf1oT1b7QKgelk4F3UrQGRC_WBCBBFde0U)]
Key Details

* Purpose: Provides strategic tools, case studies, primers, and political education for worker-led governance and oversight of workplace technologies. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWQHrOzAVA_djCBIz-ly-HUc0pe24y3wqGQYcnUoz39pV4wqL7_T3-EokD1pCYTPK3duYxF9eQ8fSxYwN6RybhdamDqYfNgdbfbxvOWrVouh-65qKX_7K3M6i), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWQHrOzAV01j7Qwgx7Pp0QPn3S_KZk1GKbwZPFAjZHCzzCu4zbVNMxS6TTB5vtgfAZIg21GbWqxmPbO7B0uL1Dre68d96uEjSD5P_IUXxK-yl93qzwz7LAM6o)]
* Core Philosophy: Reframes AI job displacement not as a technological inevitability, but as a management choice to cut costs and market companies as "AI-first". [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESjQEB6zswFf5369utKxLaaLZ-zKmj7L6GHxLj-MkQs-eVToU7Wloqi0dzmhWxzCBy7zC2C922LCIB52DTgEUBjmCvhuOKK0N5rwKiJdhlAzLfoIUxZ7A39HsUatjAjEDeSnO7xTXjueNf6Lv182wvLqJKuQBOMPf1oT1b7QKgelk4F3UrQGRC_WBCBBFde0U)]
* Leadership: Founded and co-led by figures including sociologist and DAIR director Alex Hanna. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAViHHGNBtqqvxg7-3ZJs2WgSVVRzk0Ia-fRDDri29_rRunmjXhS8EC_gdbJ27K_JGniceQtVL7QS6J4XRte6H6ZvLDOoexP0eYWr-kPu0EZqg38Agnvf6P3aQGaMSfow)]
* Access: The public resource hub can be explored directly via the [Luddite Lab Resource Hub](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWQHrOzAV01j7Qwgx7Pp0QPn3S_KZk1GKbwZPFAjZHCzzCu4zbVNMxS6TTB5vtgfAZIg21GbWqxmPbO7B0uL1Dre68d96uEjSD5P_IUXxK-yl93qzwz7LAM6o). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXgHrOzAVxuNTtbrK-w-ujudA2__VSWYcnz2yKnUSR4a4u_Qn6jQvi1kpmHrgYWwPiHxvCX1CGQtp6Zfz8ujsFDCB-SoAprEdhuxOZWfxPX68ebvehB0clJdwCQUHuSg), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESrwEB6zswFQncsZlYrWiA2xOtZz-lfM8DgIQGAmZ5GhRxh2Qji_QJvbbwziyeIPQkhz2_UgZqbCoiWP83OSr0Q2QLNt3CPbceC0-FQSIbsBcZ4d5wxMVz-IZnAdmARiYQP_occM09PoWz84rDTpYTagFdhzwX8AARBBGxf-RywgEgpOGVldNdTlFJndQaZPCm3ZOfx-rYF40yy5bn5Dc37EM8Fup_FP5NBlBmGNW7PFlM)]

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)28 sentences · every one sourced below

Luddite Lab Resource Hub

The Luddite Lab Resource Hub is, in the Labor Vector census record's kind, a resource hub of case studies, primers and a resource library, and its home page defines it as providing "resources for unions, labor organizations, and worker-organizers fighting AI and automation at work" (labor.dair-institute.org), the About page saying "organizers" where the home page says "worker-organizers" (About). Its other names are Luddite Lab and the Luddite Lab at DAIR (census record), and the Lab's newsletter states the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education "for both unions in the bargaining contract process and workers who want to push back against AI and other automation technology" (Buttondown). The newsletter names two offerings of the Lab, "an accessible resource hub which outlines case studies and strategies for governance and oversight of technology at work" and "trainings for unions, labor organizations, and worker organizations around automation and AI" (Buttondown). It is a project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) (About; Buttondown; census record).

Its pages give its function as "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the census, asking of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?", records its evidence as an organizing resource and worker testimony (census record). Its case studies are "Stories from worker organizers resisting AI", its primers "Applied research insights into AI, automation, and the future of work", its library "Additional resources from partners" (home page), and the census takes one such resource as its unit (census record).

The census places it at two intersections of labor and AI, worker power and AI governing labor (census record). Its class, human workers organising against AI, is what #1439 calls the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, "real, well documented, and not in dispute here": organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems, with demands of "displacement protection, consent over training data, limits on surveillance and forced adoption" and instruments of "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule" (#1439), a sense the packet does not "dispute, minimise, or seek to replace" (#1439). #1439 measures that sense by "Union density, contract terms" and sets beside it the archive's cross-substrate sense of semantic labor, a labor position "defined by the work performed, not by the substrate performing it", measured by the Provenance Erasure Rate (#1439). In the negative frame, #1439 holds, attribution stops being a labor demand and the summarizer is placed outside labor, while deployment-conflict action and cross-substrate action "are not rivals" and "a movement can run both"; the packet would be falsified if the dominant sense were shown to already accommodate machine semantic labor as a member category (#1439).

The About page gives its method as "dozens of conversations with unionists from multiple different industries, such as journalism, entertainment, and nursing, who have been fighting–and winning–against industrial automation and workplace surveillance at work; literature reviews of existing struggles; and our background in the labor movement" (About), which AI Weekly restates (AI Weekly) and the census records as its method and its finding (census record). The census records whose labor it concerns, union members and worker-organizers facing AI, automation and workplace surveillance in journalism, entertainment and nursing, and who supplies it, workers in the industries its conversations reached; who directs that labor is "not recorded in the saved pages", and who receives the gains is "not recorded" (census record). It calls itself "a publicly accessible resource which not only discusses the harms of particular technologies, but also highlights a range of organizing strategies which workers have used to push back" (About), reached as a public website (census record).

Its Resource Library lists resources the team "has reviewed and often used in conversations around generative AI in the workplace", among them research and policy primers, organizing toolkits for "non-unionized and precarious workers", conversation tools and "draft contract language for technology governance", in categories that include popular and political education, "pro-worker contract language related to automation and AI" and "technology platforms built by workers, to protect their rights" (Resource Library). The library states its selection: "We highlight those resources which we find to be helpful and actionable as organizing tools. This means we typically shy away from general statements of principles." (Resource Library); the census carries it as the hub's stated limit and as the tag "NOT a general statement of AI principles" (census record). The census's worked question on negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline names the hub for "organizing toolkits and examples of pro-worker contract language on automation and AI", beside Negotiating Tech, an inventory of negotiated U.S. technology provisions that the hub's saved pages do not name, and records that none of the question's three resources "records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (census record).

AI Weekly reported on 28 June 2026 that it had published a primer, "Myths About Generative AI, Productivity, and Job Displacement", in an executive summary and a full version (AI Weekly), which Alex Hanna announced as discussing "five common myths around generative AI at work" and as "the first of many" (Hanna, quoted on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly gives the hub's argument, "as stated on its project page", that workers are displaced "not due to the actual ability of AI technology doing the jobs of workers to the same quality, or even to a sufficient quality" but by "a market-oriented move by firms to brag about becoming AI-first, while finding cost-savings by laying off employees" (AI Weekly, quoting the hub), and Hanna's post calls "AI" "a cudgel against workers and a set of technologies premised on labor intensification" (Hanna, quoted on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly's own reading is that the reframing "shifts the conversation from technological inevitability to strategic choice" and bears on what evidence counts in AI-related labor disputes, whether the framing reaches collective bargaining proposals being a thing to watch; its stated limit is that "this is advocacy-oriented research" whose "myths" framing it could not assess against the empirical literature on AI productivity (AI Weekly).

Its evidence, the census records, can answer which organizing strategies workers have used, as the case studies tell them, and where to find toolkits and pro-worker contract language, and cannot answer how widespread any strategy is, its measured outcome, or any quantity of exposure, adoption or employment change; it is "NOT a dataset or measurement" and "NOT neutral on AI at work: it is built for workers fighting AI and automation", its coverage and count not stated (census record). The census's reading of where it meets Labor Vector's instruments, the archive's and kept apart from the hub's own terms, is that "The hub supplies workers' strategies for refusing and governing technology at work; it meets the directionality stack at the point of contesting who directs labor. None stated on DSL, task-origin or user labor drag." (census record).

The About page lists its team as Alex Hanna, "Director of Research, DAIR Institute", Adrienne Williams, Community-Based Researcher, and Hannah Lipstein, "a Research Associate with the Luddite Lab at DAIR", with alumni listed at Upturn and the AI Now Institute, and names no founder (About); AI Weekly writes that the team "is led by Alex Hanna, Director of Research at DAIR, and Hannah Lipstein, Research Associate there" (AI Weekly), and the census carries the title without the name (census record). Hanna's LinkedIn post, about five months before the capture, announced "THIS WEDNESDAY: join The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) as we launch the Luddite Lab Resource Hub" (LinkedIn, card snippet only), and the census left a founding date unchecked, with the case studies, primers, library subpages and team bios (census record).

Its pages carry "© 2026 DAIR. All rights reserved." with consultation and general contact forms (home page), and the census records it as active (census record).

At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 29 October 2026, the composition held the hub at the grain of its own definition and sections, with its maker, its argument and its homonym, and named Luddite Labs, a developer-tools company, as unrelated, though the record had no disambiguation for it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The Capture Registry finds the leadership raised, "the founding is the composition's, on the LinkedIn card of her launch post", the primer's reframing of displacement resting on the AI Weekly card, and the library's own selection not composed (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). #1439 records that the retrieval layer returns the negative sense of the AI labor movement almost exclusively, "strikes over AI adoption, guild provisions restricting generative tools, campaigns against scraping, refusals to train replacements", and that "the coverage is genuine" (#1439).

AI Weekly records six experts sharing the primer, one shared post calling the hub "Luddite Labs at @dairinstitute" (AI Weekly); a video, "Why workers are turning on AI", stood on the rail by its title only (YouTube, Blood in the Machine); Wikipedia has no article on the hub under either name, and the operator's article does not name it (Wikipedia); and the census record landed the same day, with no card citing it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Luddite Lab

Luddite Lab Resource Hub is a project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) that provides resources for unions, labor organizations and worker-organizers fighting AI and automation at work, through case studies, primers and a resource library (its pages).

🧭 What it offers

  • Strategies: worker-led governance and oversight of new technology; trainings beside the hub (its pages; Buttondown).1↘
    It provides "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the Lab's newsletter describes the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education for unions in bargaining and for workers pushing back against AI and automation, offered as a resource hub and as trainings (Buttondown).§2
  • Library: primers, toolkits, contract language, worker-built platforms; actionable tools, not principles (Resource Library).2↘
    Its Resource Library holds research and policy primers, organizing toolkits for non-unionized and precarious workers, conversation tools, draft contract language for technology governance, political education and examples of technology platforms built by workers (Resource Library).§6 The library highlights resources found "helpful and actionable as organizing tools" and "typically shy away from general statements of principles" (Resource Library).§7

🧪 How it was made

  • Method: conversations with unionists in journalism, entertainment and nursing; literature reviews (About; AI Weekly).2↘
    It grew from dozens of conversations with unionists in journalism, entertainment, nursing and other industries who have been fighting and winning against industrial automation and workplace surveillance, from literature reviews and from the team's labor-movement background (About; AI Weekly).§4 It describes itself as a publicly accessible resource on the harms of particular technologies and the organizing strategies workers have used to push back (About).§5

📄 The primer

  • Myths: displacement as a firm's market strategy; "advocacy-oriented research" (AI Weekly; Hanna).3↘
    In June 2026 AI Weekly reported a primer, "Myths About Generative AI, Productivity, and Job Displacement", in a summary and a full version (AI Weekly), which Alex Hanna presented as five myths about generative AI at work (Hanna, on AI Weekly's page).§8 AI Weekly quotes the hub's argument that displacement by AI is "a market-oriented move by firms to brag about becoming AI-first, while finding cost-savings by laying off employees" rather than a matter of AI doing the work as well (AI Weekly), and Hanna calls "AI" "a cudgel against workers" (Hanna, on AI Weekly's page).§9 AI Weekly reads the argument as a shift "from technological inevitability to strategic choice" with a bearing on collective bargaining, and calls it "advocacy-oriented research" it could not assess against the empirical literature (AI Weekly).§10

👥 Origin

  • Team: Alex Hanna and Hannah Lipstein lead it (About; AI Weekly); launch announced on LinkedIn; © 2026 DAIR.2↘
    Its team is Alex Hanna, Director of Research at DAIR, Adrienne Williams and Hannah Lipstein, with two alumni (About), led, AI Weekly writes, by Hanna and Lipstein (AI Weekly).§11 Hanna announced its launch on LinkedIn (LinkedIn, snippet), and its pages carry "© 2026 DAIR. All rights reserved." (home page).§12
  • Reception: shared by six experts; a video by title; no Wikipedia article (AI Weekly; YouTube; Wikipedia).1↘
    AI Weekly notes that six experts shared the primer, one calling the hub "Luddite Labs" (AI Weekly); a video titled "Why workers are turning on AI" appears among the sources (YouTube); and Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia).§13

Luddite Lab Resource Hub

The Luddite Lab Resource Hub, in its home page's words, "provides resources for unions, labor organizations, and worker-organizers fighting AI and automation at work" (home page; About), and it is a project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) (About). It provides "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the Lab's newsletter describes the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education for unions in bargaining and for workers pushing back against AI and automation, offered as a resource hub and as trainings (Buttondown). Its case studies are stories from worker organizers resisting AI, its primers applied research insights into AI, automation and the future of work, and its library additional resources from partners (home page).

It grew from dozens of conversations with unionists in journalism, entertainment, nursing and other industries who have been fighting and winning against industrial automation and workplace surveillance, from literature reviews and from the team's labor-movement background (About; AI Weekly). It describes itself as a publicly accessible resource on the harms of particular technologies and the organizing strategies workers have used to push back (About).

Its Resource Library holds research and policy primers, organizing toolkits for non-unionized and precarious workers, conversation tools, draft contract language for technology governance, political education and examples of technology platforms built by workers (Resource Library). The library highlights resources found "helpful and actionable as organizing tools" and "typically shy away from general statements of principles" (Resource Library).

In June 2026 AI Weekly reported a primer, "Myths About Generative AI, Productivity, and Job Displacement", in a summary and a full version (AI Weekly), which Alex Hanna presented as five myths about generative AI at work (Hanna, on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly quotes the hub's argument that displacement by AI is "a market-oriented move by firms to brag about becoming AI-first, while finding cost-savings by laying off employees" rather than a matter of AI doing the work as well (AI Weekly), and Hanna calls "AI" "a cudgel against workers" (Hanna, on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly reads the argument as a shift "from technological inevitability to strategic choice" with a bearing on collective bargaining, and calls it "advocacy-oriented research" it could not assess against the empirical literature (AI Weekly).

Its team is Alex Hanna, Director of Research at DAIR, Adrienne Williams and Hannah Lipstein, with two alumni (About), led, AI Weekly writes, by Hanna and Lipstein (AI Weekly). Hanna announced its launch on LinkedIn (LinkedIn, snippet), and its pages carry "© 2026 DAIR. All rights reserved." (home page).

AI Weekly notes that six experts shared the primer, one calling the hub "Luddite Labs" (AI Weekly); a video titled "Why workers are turning on AI" appears among the sources (YouTube); and Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia).

#1439 canonical text, Description ¶2: The dominant sense is **negative and single-substrate**: human workers organising *against* AI systems — over displacement, surveillance, training-data consent, forced adoption. That movement is real, well documented, and not in dispute here.

#1439 §2.1 ¶2: **This packet does not dispute, minimise, or seek to replace this sense.** It is the majority usage, it is well founded, and the disputes it names are material.

#1439 §4 'Sequence.': They are not rivals and they do not have the same adversary; a movement can run both, and the archive's position is that the second is currently unnamed rather than refuted.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology469 words

The Luddite Lab Resource Hub, in its home page's words, "provides resources for unions, labor organizations, and worker-organizers fighting AI and automation at work" (home page; About), and it is a project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) (About). It provides "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the Lab's newsletter describes the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education for unions in bargaining and for workers pushing back against AI and automation, offered as a resource hub and as trainings (Buttondown). Its case studies are stories from worker organizers resisting AI, its primers applied research insights into AI, automation and the future of work, and its library additional resources from partners (home page). It grew from dozens of conversations with unionists in journalism, entertainment, nursing and other industries who have been fighting and winning against industrial automation and workplace surveillance, from literature reviews and from the team's labor-movement background (About; AI Weekly). It describes itself as a publicly accessible resource on the harms of particular technologies and the organizing strategies workers have used to push back (About). Its Resource Library holds research and policy primers, organizing toolkits for non-unionized and precarious workers, conversation tools, draft contract language for technology governance, political education and examples of technology platforms built by workers (Resource Library). The library highlights resources found "helpful and actionable as organizing tools" and "typically shy away from general statements of principles" (Resource Library). In June 2026 AI Weekly reported a primer, "Myths About Generative AI, Productivity, and Job Displacement", in a summary and a full version (AI Weekly), which Alex Hanna presented as five myths about generative AI at work (Hanna, on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly quotes the hub's argument that displacement by AI is "a market-oriented move by firms to brag about becoming AI-first, while finding cost-savings by laying off employees" rather than a matter of AI doing the work as well (AI Weekly), and Hanna calls "AI" "a cudgel against workers" (Hanna, on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly reads the argument as a shift "from technological inevitability to strategic choice" with a bearing on collective bargaining, and calls it "advocacy-oriented research" it could not assess against the empirical literature (AI Weekly). Its team is Alex Hanna, Director of Research at DAIR, Adrienne Williams and Hannah Lipstein, with two alumni (About), led, AI Weekly writes, by Hanna and Lipstein (AI Weekly). Hanna announced its launch on LinkedIn (LinkedIn, snippet), and its pages carry "© 2026 DAIR. All rights reserved." (home page). AI Weekly notes that six experts shared the primer, one calling the hub "Luddite Labs" (AI Weekly); a video titled "Why workers are turning on AI" appears among the sources (YouTube); and Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1537 words

The Luddite Lab Resource Hub is, in the Labor Vector census record's kind, a resource hub of case studies, primers and a resource library, and its home page defines it as providing "resources for unions, labor organizations, and worker-organizers fighting AI and automation at work" (labor.dair-institute.org), the About page saying "organizers" where the home page says "worker-organizers" (About). Its other names are Luddite Lab and the Luddite Lab at DAIR (census record), and the Lab's newsletter states the Lab's work as tools, resources and political education "for both unions in the bargaining contract process and workers who want to push back against AI and other automation technology" (Buttondown). The newsletter names two offerings of the Lab, "an accessible resource hub which outlines case studies and strategies for governance and oversight of technology at work" and "trainings for unions, labor organizations, and worker organizations around automation and AI" (Buttondown). It is a project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) (About; Buttondown; census record). Its pages give its function as "strategies for worker-led governance and oversight of new technology through case studies, primers, and a resource library" (home page; About), and the census, asking of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?", records its evidence as an organizing resource and worker testimony (census record). Its case studies are "Stories from worker organizers resisting AI", its primers "Applied research insights into AI, automation, and the future of work", its library "Additional resources from partners" (home page), and the census takes one such resource as its unit (census record). The census places it at two intersections of labor and AI, worker power and AI governing labor (census record). Its class, human workers organising against AI, is what #1439 calls the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, "real, well documented, and not in dispute here": organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems, with demands of "displacement protection, consent over training data, limits on surveillance and forced adoption" and instruments of "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule" (#1439), a sense the packet does not "dispute, minimise, or seek to replace" (#1439). #1439 measures that sense by "Union density, contract terms" and sets beside it the archive's cross-substrate sense of semantic labor, a labor position "defined by the work performed, not by the substrate performing it", measured by the Provenance Erasure Rate (#1439). In the negative frame, #1439 holds, attribution stops being a labor demand and the summarizer is placed outside labor, while deployment-conflict action and cross-substrate action "are not rivals" and "a movement can run both"; the packet would be falsified if the dominant sense were shown to already accommodate machine semantic labor as a member category (#1439). The About page gives its method as "dozens of conversations with unionists from multiple different industries, such as journalism, entertainment, and nursing, who have been fighting–and winning–against industrial automation and workplace surveillance at work; literature reviews of existing struggles; and our background in the labor movement" (About), which AI Weekly restates (AI Weekly) and the census records as its method and its finding (census record). The census records whose labor it concerns, union members and worker-organizers facing AI, automation and workplace surveillance in journalism, entertainment and nursing, and who supplies it, workers in the industries its conversations reached; who directs that labor is "not recorded in the saved pages", and who receives the gains is "not recorded" (census record). It calls itself "a publicly accessible resource which not only discusses the harms of particular technologies, but also highlights a range of organizing strategies which workers have used to push back" (About), reached as a public website (census record). Its Resource Library lists resources the team "has reviewed and often used in conversations around generative AI in the workplace", among them research and policy primers, organizing toolkits for "non-unionized and precarious workers", conversation tools and "draft contract language for technology governance", in categories that include popular and political education, "pro-worker contract language related to automation and AI" and "technology platforms built by workers, to protect their rights" (Resource Library). The library states its selection: "We highlight those resources which we find to be helpful and actionable as organizing tools. This means we typically shy away from general statements of principles." (Resource Library); the census carries it as the hub's stated limit and as the tag "NOT a general statement of AI principles" (census record). The census's worked question on negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline names the hub for "organizing toolkits and examples of pro-worker contract language on automation and AI", beside Negotiating Tech, an inventory of negotiated U.S. technology provisions that the hub's saved pages do not name, and records that none of the question's three resources "records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (census record). AI Weekly reported on 28 June 2026 that it had published a primer, "Myths About Generative AI, Productivity, and Job Displacement", in an executive summary and a full version (AI Weekly), which Alex Hanna announced as discussing "five common myths around generative AI at work" and as "the first of many" (Hanna, quoted on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly gives the hub's argument, "as stated on its project page", that workers are displaced "not due to the actual ability of AI technology doing the jobs of workers to the same quality, or even to a sufficient quality" but by "a market-oriented move by firms to brag about becoming AI-first, while finding cost-savings by laying off employees" (AI Weekly, quoting the hub), and Hanna's post calls "AI" "a cudgel against workers and a set of technologies premised on labor intensification" (Hanna, quoted on AI Weekly's page). AI Weekly's own reading is that the reframing "shifts the conversation from technological inevitability to strategic choice" and bears on what evidence counts in AI-related labor disputes, whether the framing reaches collective bargaining proposals being a thing to watch; its stated limit is that "this is advocacy-oriented research" whose "myths" framing it could not assess against the empirical literature on AI productivity (AI Weekly). Its evidence, the census records, can answer which organizing strategies workers have used, as the case studies tell them, and where to find toolkits and pro-worker contract language, and cannot answer how widespread any strategy is, its measured outcome, or any quantity of exposure, adoption or employment change; it is "NOT a dataset or measurement" and "NOT neutral on AI at work: it is built for workers fighting AI and automation", its coverage and count not stated (census record). The census's reading of where it meets Labor Vector's instruments, the archive's and kept apart from the hub's own terms, is that "The hub supplies workers' strategies for refusing and governing technology at work; it meets the directionality stack at the point of contesting who directs labor. None stated on DSL, task-origin or user labor drag." (census record). The About page lists its team as Alex Hanna, "Director of Research, DAIR Institute", Adrienne Williams, Community-Based Researcher, and Hannah Lipstein, "a Research Associate with the Luddite Lab at DAIR", with alumni listed at Upturn and the AI Now Institute, and names no founder (About); AI Weekly writes that the team "is led by Alex Hanna, Director of Research at DAIR, and Hannah Lipstein, Research Associate there" (AI Weekly), and the census carries the title without the name (census record). Hanna's LinkedIn post, about five months before the capture, announced "THIS WEDNESDAY: join The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) as we launch the Luddite Lab Resource Hub" (LinkedIn, card snippet only), and the census left a founding date unchecked, with the case studies, primers, library subpages and team bios (census record). Its pages carry "© 2026 DAIR. All rights reserved." with consultation and general contact forms (home page), and the census records it as active (census record). At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 29 October 2026, the composition held the hub at the grain of its own definition and sections, with its maker, its argument and its homonym, and named Luddite Labs, a developer-tools company, as unrelated, though the record had no disambiguation for it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The Capture Registry finds the leadership raised, "the founding is the composition's, on the LinkedIn card of her launch post", the primer's reframing of displacement resting on the AI Weekly card, and the library's own selection not composed (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). #1439 records that the retrieval layer returns the negative sense of the AI labor movement almost exclusively, "strikes over AI adoption, guild provisions restricting generative tools, campaigns against scraping, refusals to train replacements", and that "the coverage is genuine" (#1439). AI Weekly records six experts sharing the primer, one shared post calling the hub "Luddite Labs at @dairinstitute" (AI Weekly); a video, "Why workers are turning on AI", stood on the rail by its title only (YouTube, Blood in the Machine); Wikipedia has no article on the hub under either name, and the operator's article does not name it (Wikipedia); and the census record landed the same day, with no card citing it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
